claim: HBV infection accounts for 300 million chronic infections each year.
source: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is estimated to account for 300 million chronic infections and 1 million deaths each year (World Health Organization, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2021

claim: HBV infection accounts for 1 million deaths each year.
source: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is estimated to account for 300 million chronic infections and 1 million deaths each year (World Health Organization, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2021

claim: The global burden of HBV infection is unevenly distributed, with particularly high prevalence in some populations in Africa and South East Asia.
source: The global burden of HBV infection is unevenly distributed, with particularly high prevalence in some populations in Africa and South East Asia (Cooke et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cooke et al., 2019

claim: HBV disproportionately affects marginalised and deprived populations whose needs are poorly met by existing healthcare research, services, interventions and policies.
source: Likewise, HBV is not experienced equally across society, with a disproportionate prevalence and impact on marginalised and deprived populations, whose needs are poorly met by existing healthcare research, services, interventions and policies (O'Hara et al., 2017; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Hara et al., 2017

claim: Only an estimated 10% of those living with HBV infection are diagnosed.
source: Silent infection, in combination with barriers to testing in the most affected populations, explains why only an estimated 10% of those living with HBV infection are diagnosed (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Hara et al., 2017

claim: In 2022, projected US funding for HIV research is 20-fold greater than for HBV.
source: For example, in 2022, projected US funding for HIV research is 20-fold greater than for HBV, despite the lower number of people living with HIV infection (National institutes of health, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to National institutes of health, 2022

claim: There are 1.5 million new HBV infections each year.
source: Therefore, HBV remains a major public health threat, with 1.5 million new infections each year and more annual deaths than malaria or HIV (O'Hara et al., 2017, Graber-Stiehl, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Hara et al., 2017 and Graber-Stiehl, 2018

claim: HBV causes more annual deaths than malaria or HIV.
source: Therefore, HBV remains a major public health threat, with 1.5 million new infections each year and more annual deaths than malaria or HIV (O'Hara et al., 2017, Graber-Stiehl, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Hara et al., 2017 and Graber-Stiehl, 2018

claim: By the end of 2020, there were 281 million international migrants, equivalent to 3.6% of the world's population.
source: By the end of 2020, there were 281 million international migrants, equivalent to 3.6% of the world's population (International organisation for migration, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to International organisation for migration, 2021

claim: Approximately 90 million migrants are displaced due to conflict, political instability, and natural disasters.
source: A significant proportion (approaching 90 million) are displaced due to conflict, political instability, and natural disasters.
evidence: Stated as a factual assertion in the manuscript text

claim: In Europe, more than half of 49 million migrants born outside of the European Economic Area came from nations where HBV endemicity is either intermediate (2–8%) or high (>8%).
source: In Europe, more than half of 49 million migrants born outside of the European Economic Area came from nations where HBV endemicity is either intermediate (2–8%) or high (>8%), explaining the higher prevalence of HBV infection in migrants (5%), and asylum seekers (10%) compared to the general population (1%) in Europe (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2016; Kim et al., 2021; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2016 and Kim et al., 2021

claim: HBV prevalence in migrants in Europe is 5%.
source: In Europe, more than half of 49 million migrants born outside of the European Economic Area came from nations where HBV endemicity is either intermediate (2–8%) or high (>8%), explaining the higher prevalence of HBV infection in migrants (5%), and asylum seekers (10%) compared to the general population (1%) in Europe (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2016; Kim et al., 2021; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2016 and Kim et al., 2021

claim: HBV prevalence in asylum seekers in Europe is 10%.
source: In Europe, more than half of 49 million migrants born outside of the European Economic Area came from nations where HBV endemicity is either intermediate (2–8%) or high (>8%), explaining the higher prevalence of HBV infection in migrants (5%), and asylum seekers (10%) compared to the general population (1%) in Europe (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2016; Kim et al., 2021; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2016 and Kim et al., 2021

claim: HBV prevalence in the general population in Europe is 1%.
source: In Europe, more than half of 49 million migrants born outside of the European Economic Area came from nations where HBV endemicity is either intermediate (2–8%) or high (>8%), explaining the higher prevalence of HBV infection in migrants (5%), and asylum seekers (10%) compared to the general population (1%) in Europe (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2016; Kim et al., 2021; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2016 and Kim et al., 2021

claim: Approximately 150 million people worldwide were considered homeless in 2020.
source: Approximately 150 million people worldwide were considered homeless in 2020 (Chamie, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chamie, 2017

claim: People experiencing homelessness have substantially increased mortality from any cause compared to a socially deprived population.
source: People experiencing homelessness (PEH) endure extreme social exclusion and have substantially increased mortality from any cause compared to a socially deprived population (Table 2; Aldridge et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aldridge et al., 2018 and reference to Table 2

claim: Seroprevalence surveys report higher HBV seroprevalence among people experiencing homelessness compared to the housed population.
source: Seroprevalence surveys, although of varying size and quality, report higher HBV seroprevalence among PEH compared to the housed population (Ly et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ly et al., 2021a

claim: There are an estimated 15.6 million People Who Inject Drugs (PWID) between the ages of 15–64 years worldwide.
source: It is estimated that there are 15.6 million People Who Inject Drugs (PWID) between the ages of 15–64 years worldwide (Degenhardt et al., 2017), while an estimated 283 million people have alcohol use disorders (World Health Organization, 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Degenhardt et al., 2017

claim: An estimated 283 million people have alcohol use disorders.
source: It is estimated that there are 15.6 million People Who Inject Drugs (PWID) between the ages of 15–64 years worldwide (Degenhardt et al., 2017), while an estimated 283 million people have alcohol use disorders (World Health Organization, 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2018a

claim: HBV infection disproportionately affects people who misuse drugs and alcohol.
source: HBV infection disproportionately affects people who misuse drugs and alcohol (Table 2; Degenhardt et al., 2017; Magri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Degenhardt et al., 2017 and Magri et al., 2020, and reference to Table 2

claim: Alcohol use is associated with increased high-risk sexual activity, drug use, and sharing injecting equipment.
source: Alcohol use is associated with increased high-risk sexual activity, drug use, and sharing injecting equipment, and therefore may increase risk of HBV transmission (Arasteh et al., 2008), while alcohol acts synergistically with HBV infection to accelerate liver damage (Gitto et al., 2009; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arasteh et al., 2008

claim: Alcohol acts synergistically with HBV infection to accelerate liver damage.
source: Alcohol use is associated with increased high-risk sexual activity, drug use, and sharing injecting equipment, and therefore may increase risk of HBV transmission (Arasteh et al., 2008), while alcohol acts synergistically with HBV infection to accelerate liver damage (Gitto et al., 2009; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gitto et al., 2009 and Li et al., 2019

claim: At the end of 2021, the worldwide prison population was at least 10.77 million.
source: At the end of 2021, the worldwide prison population was at least 10.77 million (Fair and Walmsley, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fair and Walmsley, 2021

claim: The estimated global HBsAg prevalence in incarcerated individuals is 4.8%.
source: Nevertheless, HBV is over-represented in incarcerated individuals, with an estimated global HBsAg prevalence of 4.8% (Dolan et al., 2016; Nakitanda et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dolan et al., 2016 and Nakitanda et al., 2021

claim: 25% of PWID report initiating drug use in prisons.
source: 25% of PWID report initiating drug use in prisons and incarceration is associated with a doubled risk of re-initiating injecting drug use (Genberg et al., 2015; Kamarulzaman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Genberg et al., 2015 and Kamarulzaman et al., 2016

claim: Incarceration is associated with a doubled risk of re-initiating injecting drug use.
source: 25% of PWID report initiating drug use in prisons and incarceration is associated with a doubled risk of re-initiating injecting drug use (Genberg et al., 2015; Kamarulzaman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Genberg et al., 2015 and Kamarulzaman et al., 2016

claim: Frequency and duration of incarceration are positively associated with prevalence of HBV infection.
source: Frequency and duration of incarceration are also positively associated with prevalence of HBV infection (Dana et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dana et al., 2013

claim: Sex workers are underrepresented in the literature and robust data are lacking.
source: Sex workers are underrepresented in the literature and robust data are lacking (Aldridge et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aldridge et al., 2018

claim: In Europe, Roma and Traveller populations number 10–12 million.
source: In Europe, these populations number 10–12 million, but this is likely to be an underestimate due to high mobility and poor data capture (Council of Europe, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Council of Europe, 2020

claim: Roma and Traveller communities have a 10-year lower life expectancy than the settled population in the UK.
source: These communities experiences extreme health disparities, with a 10-year lower life expectancy than the settled population in the UK (Equality and Human Rights Commission, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Equality and Human Rights Commission, 2017

claim: In the UK, a study of Roma people found a HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) prevalence of 9.4%.
source: HBV is not well studied among these populations, but in the UK a study of Roma people found a HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) prevalence of 9.4% and in Eastern Slovakia, Roma community members were four times more likely to be HBsAg-positive compared to the age-matched general population (Macejova et al., 2020; Gregory et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Macejova et al., 2020 and Gregory et al., 2014

claim: In Eastern Slovakia, Roma community members were four times more likely to be HBsAg-positive compared to the age-matched general population.
source: HBV is not well studied among these populations, but in the UK a study of Roma people found a HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) prevalence of 9.4% and in Eastern Slovakia, Roma community members were four times more likely to be HBsAg-positive compared to the age-matched general population (Macejova et al., 2020; Gregory et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Macejova et al., 2020 and Gregory et al., 2014

claim: Aboriginal Australians have a higher HBV prevalence, higher rate of liver disease, and poorer outcomes, compared to non-Indigenous Australians.
source: For example, Aboriginal Australians have a higher HBV prevalence, higher rate of liver disease, and poorer outcomes, compared to non-Indigenous Australians (Plackett, 2022; Qama et al., 2021; Wigg et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Plackett, 2022; Qama et al., 2021; and Wigg et al., 2021

claim: HBV genotype C4 in Aboriginal Australians is associated with aggressive disease progression.
source: HBV genotype may also be an important consideration; genotype C4 in Aboriginal Australians is associated with aggressive disease progression, however this impact is yet to be unpicked from the effects of social determinants of health (Davies et al., 2019; Plackett, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davies et al., 2019 and Plackett, 2022

claim: Current HBV vaccine, which is designed against genotype A, may have reduced efficacy against genotype C4.
source: In addition, there is some evidence that current HBV vaccine, which is designed against genotype A, may have reduced efficacy against C4 (Qama et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Qama et al., 2021

claim: HBV infection was twice as likely in female migrants in Italy.
source: For example, HBV infection was twice as likely in female migrants in Italy, and a higher proportion of female migrants and unaccompanied asylum-seeking children report a history of sexual assault/abuse which represents a significant HBV transmission risk (Prestileo et al., 2022, Armitage et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Prestileo et al., 2022 and Armitage et al., 2022

claim: Being female was associated with lower HBV vaccination uptake in PEH, PWID and people with a history of incarceration in the UK.
source: Being female was associated with lower HBV vaccination uptake in PEH, PWID and people with a history of incarceration in the UK (Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2019

claim: HBV prevalence in pregnancy was significantly higher in undocumented migrants than in the general population in Finland.
source: A Finnish study found that HBV prevalence in pregnancy was significantly higher in undocumented migrants than in the general population.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tasa et al., 2021 in Table 2

claim: Most pregnant migrants in Finland entered antenatal care late, and either received inadequate care or none at all.
source: Most pregnant migrants entered antenatal care late, and either received inadequate care or none at all (Tasa et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tasa et al., 2021

claim: Pregnant migrant women in Thailand had very low levels of HBV knowledge.
source: Education and awareness are also lacking among women in some inclusion health populations: pregnant migrant women in Thailand had very low levels of HBV knowledge (Bierhoff et al., 2021), and despite a high prevalence of HBV (8%), more than 90% of FSW in Mumbai had not heard of HBV infection (United Way Mumbai, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bierhoff et al., 2021

claim: More than 90% of FSW in Mumbai had not heard of HBV infection despite a high prevalence of HBV (8%).
source: Education and awareness are also lacking among women in some inclusion health populations: pregnant migrant women in Thailand had very low levels of HBV knowledge (Bierhoff et al., 2021), and despite a high prevalence of HBV (8%), more than 90% of FSW in Mumbai had not heard of HBV infection (United Way Mumbai, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to United Way Mumbai, 2017

claim: Female standardised mortality ratio in inclusion health populations is 11.86 (95% CI 10.42–13.3; I2 91.5%).
source: This female disadvantage observed in inclusion health populations with HBV is reflected in the dramatically increased all-cause mortality in females compared to males across the wider inclusion health population, with female standardised mortality ratio (SMR) 11.86 (95% CI 10.42–13.3; I2 91.5%) vs. Male SMR 7.88 (95% CI 6.40–9.37; I2 98.1%) (Aldridge et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aldridge et al., 2018

claim: Male standardised mortality ratio in inclusion health populations is 7.88 (95% CI 6.40–9.37; I2 98.1%).
source: This female disadvantage observed in inclusion health populations with HBV is reflected in the dramatically increased all-cause mortality in females compared to males across the wider inclusion health population, with female standardised mortality ratio (SMR) 11.86 (95% CI 10.42–13.3; I2 91.5%) vs. Male SMR 7.88 (95% CI 6.40–9.37; I2 98.1%) (Aldridge et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aldridge et al., 2018

claim: Males have worse HBV outcomes than females in the wider population, with higher rates of exposure, chronicity and complications.
source: These observations within inclusion health populations contrast with observations from the wider population, which suggest males have worse HBV outcomes than females, with higher rates of exposure, chronicity and complications (Brown et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2022

claim: A safe, effective vaccine against HBV has been available since 1982.
source: A safe, effective vaccine against HBV has been available since 1982, and remains a key tool for the elimination of viral hepatitis (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2017

claim: The WHO has recommended a universal birth dose HBV vaccination since 2009.
source: The WHO has recommended a universal birth dose HBV vaccination since 2009, irrespective of the mother's serological status, but coverage was still only 42% globally and 17% in the WHO African Region by 2021 (World Health Organization, 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022a

claim: Birth dose HBV vaccine coverage was only 42% globally by 2021.
source: The WHO has recommended a universal birth dose HBV vaccination since 2009, irrespective of the mother's serological status, but coverage was still only 42% globally and 17% in the WHO African Region by 2021 (World Health Organization, 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022a

claim: Birth dose HBV vaccine coverage was 17% in the WHO African Region by 2021.
source: The WHO has recommended a universal birth dose HBV vaccination since 2009, irrespective of the mother's serological status, but coverage was still only 42% globally and 17% in the WHO African Region by 2021 (World Health Organization, 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022a

claim: Scaling up of a timely birth dose vaccine to >90% by 2030 would result in 710,000 fewer deaths in those born between 2020–2030, globally.
source: Modelling suggests that scaling up of a timely birth dose vaccine to >90% by 2030 would result in immediate reduction of chronic HBV incidence, and 710,000 fewer deaths in those born between 2020–2030, globally (de Villiers et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Villiers et al., 2021

claim: Only 25–35% of adults with CHB are eligible for treatment according to current guidelines.
source: According to current guidelines, only 25–35% of adults with CHB are eligible for treatment, leaving the majority at risk of both longer term complications (relevant to the individual) and the potential for transmission (relevant to populations) (McNaughton et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to McNaughton et al., 2021

claim: HBV/HIV co-infected individuals may have a treatment advantage, reflecting the benefits of greater access to early and consistent antiviral treatment compared to mono-infected individuals.
source: HBV/HIV co-infected individuals may have a treatment advantage, reflecting the benefits of greater access to early and consistent antiviral treatment compared to mono-infected individuals (Maponga et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maponga et al., 2020

claim: Integrated infection screening can be cost-effective and an efficient use of resources.
source: Integrated infectious disease screening can be cost-effective and an efficient use of resources.
evidence: Stated as a factual assertion in the manuscript text

claim: The World Health Organization's 'triple elimination initiative' encourages countries to simultaneously commit to elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and HBV.
source: An example is the World Health Organization's 'triple elimination initiative' which encourages countries to simultaneously commit to elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and HBV (World Health Organization, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022b

claim: The triple elimination approach has been demonstrated to reduce disease transmission rates, staff and patient time, and overall programme cost.
source: This approach has been demonstrated to reduce disease transmission rates, staff and patient time, and overall programme cost (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019

claim: Incarcerated individuals with HBV have high rates of HIV, HCV and/or TB co-infection.
source: Multi-morbidity is common, for example, incarcerated individuals with HBV have high rates of HIV, HCV and /or TB co-infection (Ahmadi Gharaei et al., 2021; do Nascimento et al., 2020; La Torre et al., 2007), and of substance use and severe mental illness (Kamarulzaman et al., 2016; Fazel and Danesh, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ahmadi Gharaei et al., 2021; do Nascimento et al., 2020; and La Torre et al., 2007

claim: People experiencing homelessness have a three-fold elevated risk of cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular mortality compared to non-homeless individuals.
source: Non-communicable diseases are also prevalent among inclusion health populations (Tweed et al., 2021) for example, PEH have a three-fold elevated risk of cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular mortality compared to non-homeless individuals (Table 2; Al Shakarchi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Al Shakarchi et al., 2020 and reference to Table 2

claim: Diabetes is associated with an increased risk of HBV-associated HCC (hazard ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.23–1.49).
source: Diabetes is associated with an increased risk of HBV-associated HCC (hazard ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.23–1.49)(Campbell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2021

claim: Vaccination against HBV is estimated to have prevented 310 million cases of HBV infection between 1990 and 2020.
source: Vaccination against HBV, including universal birth dose administration, is a key elimination strategy and is estimated to have prevented 310 million cases of HBV infection between 1990 and 2020 (Cooke et al., 2019, de Villiers et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cooke et al., 2019 and de Villiers et al., 2021

claim: Chronic HBV infection usually remains asymptomatic until late complications (liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma).
source: Chronic HBV infection usually remains asymptomatic until late complications (liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)).
evidence: Stated as established medical knowledge

claim: Antivirals (nucleos(t)ide analogue agents) can suppress HBV viral replication.
source: There is no cure for HBV, but antivirals (nucleos(t)ide analogue agents) can suppress viral replication.
evidence: Stated as established medical knowledge

claim: There is no cure for HBV.
source: There is no cure for HBV, but antivirals (nucleos(t)ide analogue agents) can suppress viral replication.
evidence: Stated as established medical knowledge

claim: Multiple studies have demonstrated cost-effectiveness of HBV screening in a variety of different scenarios, including community-based outreach and low prevalence settings.
source: Multiple studies have demonstrated cost-effectiveness of HBV screening in a variety of different scenarios, including community-based outreach and low prevalence settings (Su et al., 2022, Xiao et al., 2020, Toy et al., 2022, Nayagam et al., 2016, Tordrup et al., 2020, Hutton et al., 2022, Wright et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Su et al., 2022, Xiao et al., 2020, Toy et al., 2022, Nayagam et al., 2016, Tordrup et al., 2020, Hutton et al., 2022, and Wright et al., 2018

claim: Cost-effectiveness of HBV screening is largely due to averting high costs associated with decompensated cirrhosis, HCC and liver transplantation.
source: This is largely due to averting high costs associated with decompensated cirrhosis, HCC and liver transplantation.
evidence: Stated as inference from the cost-effectiveness studies cited

claim: The ECDC recommends universal screening in emergency departments in areas where HBV prevalence exceeds 2%.
source: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) recommends universal screening in emergency departments in areas where HBV prevalence exceeds 2%, however, evidence suggests that universal emergency department screening is cost effective even at lower prevalence (>0.25%) and therefore the United Kingdom is currently implementing this policy (Williams et al., 2020b, Nebbia et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated as ECDC recommendation

claim: Universal emergency department screening is cost effective even at HBV prevalence >0.25%.
source: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) recommends universal screening in emergency departments in areas where HBV prevalence exceeds 2%, however, evidence suggests that universal emergency department screening is cost effective even at lower prevalence (>0.25%) and therefore the United Kingdom is currently implementing this policy (Williams et al., 2020b, Nebbia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2020b and Nebbia et al., 2022

claim: The United Kingdom is currently implementing universal emergency department screening for HBV.
source: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) recommends universal screening in emergency departments in areas where HBV prevalence exceeds 2%, however, evidence suggests that universal emergency department screening is cost effective even at lower prevalence (>0.25%) and therefore the United Kingdom is currently implementing this policy (Williams et al., 2020b, Nebbia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2020b and Nebbia et al., 2022

claim: All pregnant women should be screened for HBV.
source: All pregnant women should be screened for HBV, and healthcare professionals should consider opportunistically offering HBV screening in high-risk groups accessing services (World Health Organization, 2020; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2020 and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2022

claim: Outreach screening services for HBV have been shown to be feasible and acceptable.
source: Such outreach screening services have been shown to be feasible and acceptable (O'Carroll et al., 2017, Carr et al., 2014), and can also be incorporated into other services (e.g. drug harm reduction programmes).
evidence: Supported by citations to O'Carroll et al., 2017 and Carr et al., 2014

claim: Community-based testing strategies for migrants are effective, with highest uptake in programmes with endorsement from the local community.
source: For migrants, community-based testing strategies are effective, with highest uptake in programmes with endorsement from the local community (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2018; Robotin and George, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2018 and Robotin and George, 2014

claim: Integrated infection screening is recommended in migrants.
source: Integrated infection screening is also recommended in migrants, and in most countries screening tests are offered following a risk assessment (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2018

claim: Screening for infectious diseases in migrants is found to be cost-effective, feasible and acceptable.
source: Screening is found to be cost-effective, feasible and acceptable, but migrants are a heterogenous group, and services should be culturally appropriate, and accommodate the possibility of fear and stigma surrounding screening and diagnosis (Seedat et al., 2018; Cinardo et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seedat et al., 2018 and Cinardo et al., 2022

claim: A UK survey of primary care practitioners found many did not believe routine testing of HBV in migrants was necessary, and national guidelines were poorly followed.
source: A UK survey of primary care practitioners found many did not believe routine testing of HBV in migrants was necessary, and national guidelines were poorly followed (Evlampidou et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evlampidou et al., 2016

claim: Qualitative research from Australia has identified lack of confidence of healthcare professionals and poor communication surrounding HBV.
source: Qualitative research from Australia has identified lack of confidence of healthcare professionals and poor communication surrounding HBV (Wallace et al., 2011; Robotin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wallace et al., 2011 and Robotin et al., 2021

claim: As part of the HepCare project, people with lived experience of HCV infection were upskilled to become equal members of the healthcare team, providing a cost-effective approach to enhancing diagnosis, linkage to care and treatment success.
source: For example, as part of the HepCare project, people with lived experience of HCV infection were upskilled to become equal members of the healthcare team, providing a cost-effective approach to enhancing diagnosis, linkage to care and treatment success (Ward et al., 2019; Surey et al., 2021; Surey et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ward et al., 2019; Surey et al., 2021; and Surey et al., 2019

claim: A focus group involving people with lived experience ranked advocacy via peer-led services as the second most important intervention behind stable housing.
source: Importantly, a focus group involving people with lived experience ranked advocacy via peer-led services as the second most important intervention behind stable housing (Luchenski et al., 2018).

claim: Viral hepatitis is recognised as a global health priority within the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 2030 (SDG30).
source: Viral hepatitis is recognised as a global health priority within the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 2030 (SDG30).

claim: SDG30 targets include 90% HBV vaccine coverage, reducing new chronic infections and new infections by 90% and attributable mortality by 65%.
source: These underpin ambitious targets including 90% HBV vaccine coverage, reducing new chronic infections and new infections by 90% and attributable mortality by 65% (Cooke et al., 2019).

claim: The 'inclusion health' agenda focuses on excluded and vulnerable populations who often experience barriers to accessing healthcare and are under-represented by research, resources, interventions, advocacy, and policy.

evidence: Stated as definition of inclusion health agenda

claim: Inclusion health groups include, but are not limited to, migrants in vulnerable situations, people experiencing homelessness, individuals with substance use disorders, commercial sex workers, incarcerated individuals, and Roma and Traveller communities.
source: These groups include, but are not limited to, migrants in vulnerable situations, people experiencing homelessness (PEH), individuals with substance use disorders, commercial sex workers (CSW), incarcerated individuals, and Roma and Traveller communities (Royal College of Physicians, 2022).

claim: In the UK, asylum seekers may be moved hundreds of miles away at short notice, disrupting any continuity of care.

claim: A fifth of PWID have experienced recent homelessness (within 1 year).

claim: Over two-thirds of PWID have a history of incarceration.
source: Finally, a fifth of PWID have experienced recent homelessness (within 1 year) and over two-thirds have a history of incarceration (Degenhardt et al., 2017; Rashti et al., 2020).

claim: The immediate period following prison release is associated with high risk of heightened sexual behaviours, and drug/alcohol use.

claim: A study of street-based female sex workers in the UK found that most did not disclose their work to a primary care practitioner.

claim: In pregnancy, 13% of street-based female sex workers in the UK sought antenatal services for the first time whilst in labour.
source: A study of street-based female sex workers (FSW) in the UK found that most did not disclose their work to a primary care practitioner, and in pregnancy, 13% sought antenatal services for the first time whilst in labour, reducing opportunities to prevent mother to child transmission of HBV.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jeal and Salisbury, 2004 in Table 2

claim: Barriers to care for female sex workers include waiting times, fear of judgement and travelling long distances for healthcare.
source: Barriers to care for FSW include waiting times, fear of judgement and travelling long distances for healthcare (Jeal and Salisbury, 2004; Mc Grath-Lone et al., 2014).

claim: Mainstream healthcare services are not inclusive towards the lifestyle and culture of travelling communities, with barriers arising through discrimination, alongside lack of fixed address and low levels of literacy.
source: Mainstream healthcare services are not inclusive towards the lifestyle and culture of travelling communities, with barriers arising through discrimination, alongside lack of fixed address and low levels of literacy (McFadden et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to McFadden et al., 2018

claim: Belief in God's will, prioritising work and family commitments over personal health, mistrust in healthcare services and everyday stigma likely contribute to underdiagnosis, undertreatment and lack of preventative measures for HBV infection in Roma and Traveller communities.
source: Belief in God's will, prioritising work and family commitments over personal health, mistrust in healthcare services and everyday stigma likely contribute to underdiagnosis, undertreatment and lack of preventative measures for HBV infection (Prestileo et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prestileo et al., 2022

claim: People with co-existing exposures (e.g., incarceration and substance use, or serious mental illness and substance use) have worse outcomes.
source: Moreover, people with co-existing exposures, for example incarceration and substance use, or serious mental illness and substance use, have worse outcomes (Tweed et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tweed et al., 2021

claim: HBV infection can result in stigma and discrimination, which is magnified when combined with the experiences of socially excluded groups.
source: HBV infection can result in stigma and discrimination, which is magnified when combined with the experiences of socially excluded groups (Matthews et al., 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matthews et al., 2022a

claim: Sharing lived experiences builds rapport, trust and equality, helping promote advocacy, build peer support networks, navigate healthcare systems and promote diagnosis and treatment of blood borne infections.
source: Sharing lived experiences builds rapport, trust and equality, helping promote advocacy, build peer support networks, navigate healthcare systems and promote diagnosis and treatment of blood borne infections (Paisi et al., 2022; Crone et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paisi et al., 2022 and Crone et al., 2022

claim: There is a long history of peer-led approaches with successful outcomes in HIV, TB and HCV.
source: There is a long history of peer-led approaches with successful outcomes in HIV, TB and HCV (Story et al., 2020; Øgård-Repål et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Story et al., 2020 and Øgård-Repål et al., 2023

claim: Among PEH, fear of judgement and stigma relating to homelessness can lead to distrust of healthcare workers and services.
source: Among PEH, fear of judgement and stigma relating to homelessness can lead to distrust of healthcare workers and services, basic needs (food, clothing and shelter) are prioritised over long-term healthcare needs, and additional barriers are common (lack of insurance, transport costs, and long waiting times in unfamiliar environments) (Crone et al., 2022; Becker and Foli, 2022; Paisi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crone et al., 2022; Becker and Foli, 2022; and Paisi et al., 2022

claim: Among PEH, basic needs (food, clothing and shelter) are prioritised over long-term healthcare needs.
source: Among PEH, fear of judgement and stigma relating to homelessness can lead to distrust of healthcare workers and services, basic needs (food, clothing and shelter) are prioritised over long-term healthcare needs, and additional barriers are common (lack of insurance, transport costs, and long waiting times in unfamiliar environments) (Crone et al., 2022; Becker and Foli, 2022; Paisi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crone et al., 2022; Becker and Foli, 2022; and Paisi et al., 2022

claim: High prevalence of co-morbid conditions (e.g., severe mental illness or substance use disorders) compounds social exclusion among PEH.
source: High prevalence of co-morbid conditions compounds social exclusion, for example severe mental illness or substance use disorders (Shepherd-Banigan, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shepherd-Banigan, 2021

claim: Perceived lack of need, competing priorities (e.g. avoiding opioid withdrawal), discrimination, stigma and difficulty in navigating health systems are reasons that PWID and people with alcohol use disorder may avoid seeking care.
source: Perceived lack of need, competing priorities (e.g. avoiding opioid withdrawal), discrimination, stigma and difficulty in navigating health systems are reasons that PWID and people with alcohol use disorder may avoid seeking care (Motavalli et al., 2021; Zewdu et al., 2019; Costa et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Motavalli et al., 2021; Zewdu et al., 2019; and Costa et al., 2020

claim: Inadequate funding for harm reduction and addiction programmes is a barrier to HBV prevention.
source: Inadequate funding for harm reduction and addiction programmes is a barrier to HBV prevention.
evidence: Stated as a factual assertion in the manuscript text

claim: Criminalisation and imprisonment of PWID exacerbates transmission and creates further barriers to consistent HBV care provision.
source: Criminalisation and imprisonment of PWID exacerbates transmission and creates further barriers to consistent HBV care provision (O'Keefe et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Keefe et al., 2017

claim: The majority of published HBV literature representing prisons consists of small cross sectional seroprevalence studies, which do not reflect the dynamic nature of prison populations.
source: The majority of published HBV literature representing prisons consists of small cross sectional seroprevalence studies, which do not reflect the dynamic nature of prison populations (Wirtz et al., 2018; Dolan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wirtz et al., 2018 and Dolan et al., 2016

claim: Prisons create a complex intersection of individual, social and environmental challenges, and have been described as a 'concentration mechanism' leading to amplification and dissemination of infectious diseases.
source: Prisons create a complex intersection of individual, social and environmental challenges, and have been described as a 'concentration mechanism' leading to amplification and dissemination of infectious diseases (Kamarulzaman et al., 2016), particularly when injecting drug use and sex work are criminalised.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kamarulzaman et al., 2016

claim: Sharing contaminated needles for injecting drugs, sharing tooth brushes, unsterile tattooing, body piercing and high-risk sexual activity represent potential routes of HBV transmission within prisons.
source: Sharing contaminated needles for injecting drugs, sharing tooth brushes, unsterile tattooing, body piercing and high-risk sexual activity also represent potential routes of HBV transmission within prisons (Kamarulzaman et al., 2016; Moazen et al., 2018; Kowo et al., 2021; Harawa et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kamarulzaman et al., 2016; Moazen et al., 2018; Kowo et al., 2021; and Harawa et al., 2010

claim: Older age, marital status, having children, fewer years in education, drug and alcohol use, meeting clients on the street and high numbers of clients are associated with HBV exposure among CSWs.
source: Older age, marital status, having children, fewer years in education, drug and alcohol use, meeting clients on the street and high numbers of clients are associated with HBV exposure among CSWs (Miranda et al., 2021; Matos et al., 2017; Todd et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miranda et al., 2021; Matos et al., 2017; and Todd et al., 2010

claim: Risk factors associated with HBV infection in Roma populations included being male, older age, tattoos, and previous imprisonment.
source: Risk factors associated with HBV infection included being male, older age, tattoos, and previous imprisonment (Veselíny et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veselíny et al., 2014

claim: A variety of factors may account for HBV disparity in Aboriginal Australians, including reduced healthcare access due to remote location, social inequalities and multi-morbidity.
source: A variety of factors may account for this disparity, including reduced healthcare access due to remote location, social inequalities and multi-morbidity (Plackett, 2022; Einsiedel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Plackett, 2022 and Einsiedel et al., 2013

claim: Indigenous populations across the globe face an increased burden and worse outcomes from HBV, and are poorly represented by existing data.
source: Although culturally and geographically distinct, indigenous populations across the globe face an increased burden and worse outcomes from HBV, and are poorly represented by existing data.
evidence: Stated as a summary assertion based on the evidence presented in the section

claim: A higher proportion of female migrants and unaccompanied asylum-seeking children report a history of sexual assault/abuse which represents a significant HBV transmission risk.
source: For example, HBV infection was twice as likely in female migrants in Italy, and a higher proportion of female migrants and unaccompanied asylum-seeking children report a history of sexual assault/abuse which represents a significant HBV transmission risk (Prestileo et al., 2022, Armitage et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Prestileo et al., 2022 and Armitage et al., 2022

claim: The sexual dimorphism in HBV outcomes may be reversed in inclusion health populations compared to the wider population.
source: Further work is needed to determine whether this sexual dimorphism is truly reversed in HBV within inclusion health populations, and highlights the importance of considering HBV within the sociodemographic context of inclusion health populations as this may affect risk stratification and targeted elimination strategies.
evidence: Inferred from the contrast between observations in inclusion health populations and the wider population

claim: The majority of existing research on inclusion health and HBV is biased towards high-income settings such as Europe and North America.
source: The majority of existing research on inclusion health and HBV is biased towards high-income settings such as Europe and North America (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Table 2

claim: Gathering relevant data on HBV in inclusion health populations in some high endemicity countries is made more difficult due to criminalisation and/or stigmatisation of these populations.
source: Gathering relevant data in some high endemicity countries, including countries in the WHO African, South-East Asian and Western Pacific regions is made more difficult due to criminalisation and/or stigmatisation of inclusion health populations for example CSW, PWID and LGBTQ+ communities.
evidence: Stated as a factual assertion in the manuscript text

claim: Available data suggest intermediate to high HBV prevalence in CSWs, PWID, and incarcerated people in African populations.
source: Depending on the sampling methods, available data suggest intermediate to high HBV prevalence in CSWs, PWID, and incarcerated people in African populations (Bitty-Anderson et al., 2021; Degenhardt et al., 2017; Dolan et al., 2016; Scheibe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bitty-Anderson et al., 2021; Degenhardt et al., 2017; Dolan et al., 2016; and Scheibe et al., 2020

claim: Fear of discrimination by healthcare workers, possible legal consequences and refusal of services are barriers deterring inclusion health populations from seeking care and remaining in longer term follow up in Africa.
source: Fear of discrimination by healthcare workers, possible legal consequences and refusal of services are just some of the barriers deterring inclusion health populations from seeking care and remaining in longer term follow up (Duby et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duby et al., 2018

claim: HBV research, advocacy, representation and investment have been neglected in Africa.
source: Increased difficulties collecting relevant data, heightened exclusion from healthcare services and increased HBV prevalence, mean it is of even greater importance to prioritise HBV in the inclusion health agenda globally, particularly in Africa where HBV research, advocacy, representation and investment have been neglected.
evidence: Stated as a factual assertion in the manuscript text

claim: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control report major data gaps for HBV, now exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic, with the worst impact in high-burden (often low income) settings.
source: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control report major data gaps, now exacerbated by the Covid-19 pandemic, with the worst impact in high-burden (often low income) settings, hampering progress towards elimination (Pley et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pley et al., 2021

claim: Good quality HBV data for inclusion health populations are lacking, mostly reporting from small, independent, cross sectional seroprevalence studies.
source: Good quality HBV data for inclusion health populations are lacking, mostly reporting from small, independent, cross sectional seroprevalence studies (summarised in Table 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Table 2

claim: Point-of-care hepatitis B surface antigen tests enable community-based diagnosis.
source: Availability of point-of-care hepatitis B surface antigen tests enable community-based diagnosis, although global efforts are needed to prioritise regular supply in resource-constrained settings (Lemoine et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemoine et al., 2015

claim: Global efforts are needed to prioritise regular supply of point-of-care HBV tests in resource-constrained settings.
source: Availability of point-of-care hepatitis B surface antigen tests enable community-based diagnosis, although global efforts are needed to prioritise regular supply in resource-constrained settings (Lemoine et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemoine et al., 2015

claim: Active targeted screening efforts are an important step towards HBV elimination.
source: Active targeted screening efforts are an important step towards HBV elimination (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2021; Lemoine et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2021 and Lemoine et al., 2015
